summary.text: For \(n=2k+1\), each potential pair represented in the zeroth matrix row is \((n-j,n+j)\), whose sum is \(2n=4k+2\); thus absence of a prime decomposition forces that row, and hence the determinant, to vanish. The nonvanishing hypothesis gives a contradiction for \(k\ge 60\), while \(1\le k<60\) is settled by an explicit finite list of prime decompositions.

full_proof.text:
Let \(A(n)\) denote the integer in A228623. Thus, for each positive integer \(n\), let \(M_n\) be the \(n\times n\) matrix whose rows and columns are indexed by \(0,1,\ldots,n-1\), and put
\[
 (M_n)_{ij}=
 \begin{cases}
 1,&\text{if both }n+i-j\text{ and }n+j-i\text{ are prime},\\
 0,&\text{otherwise}.
 \end{cases}
\]
(The displayed differences are positive for the indicated range of \(i,j\). Equivalently, they may be read as the corresponding natural-number expressions.) By definition,
\[
 A(n)=\det(M_n).
\]

Assume the conjectured nonvanishing statement
\[
  n>120\text{ and }n\text{ odd}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad A(n)\ne0.
  \tag{1}
\]
We prove that for every integer \(k>0\), the number \(4k+2\) is a sum of two primes.

First we establish the determinant observation on which the argument rests.

**Lemma.** If \(n>0\) and \(2n\) is not a sum of two primes, then \(A(n)=0\).

Indeed, consider row \(i=0\) of \(M_n\). Its entry in column \(j\), where \(0\le j<n\), is \(1\) precisely when both
\[
 n-j\qquad\text{and}\qquad n+j
\]
are prime. But because \(j<n\), natural subtraction is exact here, and
\[
 (n-j)+(n+j)=2n.
\]
Consequently, if the entry in column \(j\) were \(1\), these two numbers would be primes whose sum is \(2n\). Under the hypothesis that no such prime decomposition exists, this is impossible for every \(j\). Hence every entry in row \(0\) is zero. A square matrix with a zero row has determinant zero, so \(A(n)=\det(M_n)=0\), proving the lemma.

We now fix \(k>0\) and split into two ranges.

### The finite range \(1\le k<60\)

In this range an explicit decomposition suffices. The following table gives primes \(p,q\) for every possible \(k\), with \(p+q=4k+2\):
\[
\begin{array}{c|c@{\qquad}c|c@{\qquad}c|c}
k&(p,q)& &k&(p,q)&\\ \hline
 1&(3,3)&&21&(3,83)&&41&(3,163)\\
 2&(3,7)&&22&(7,83)&&42&(3,167)\\
 3&(3,11)&&23&(5,89)&&43&(7,167)\\
 4&(5,13)&&24&(19,79)&&44&(5,173)\\
 5&(3,19)&&25&(5,97)&&45&(3,179)\\
 6&(3,23)&&26&(3,103)&&46&(5,181)\\
 7&(7,23)&&27&(3,107)&&47&(11,179)\\
 8&(3,31)&&28&(5,109)&&48&(3,191)\\
 9&(7,31)&&29&(5,113)&&49&(5,193)\\
10&(5,37)&&30&(13,109)&&50&(3,199)\\
11&(3,43)&&31&(13,113)&&51&(7,199)\\
12&(3,47)&&32&(3,127)&&52&(11,199)\\
13&(7,47)&&33&(3,131)&&53&(3,211)\\
14&(5,53)&&34&(7,131)&&54&(7,211)\\
15&(3,59)&&35&(3,139)&&55&(11,211)\\
16&(5,61)&&36&(7,139)&&56&(3,223)\\
17&(3,67)&&37&(11,139)&&57&(3,227)\\
18&(3,71)&&38&(3,151)&&58&(5,229)\\
19&(5,73)&&39&(7,151)&&59&(5,233)\\
20&(3,79)&&40&(5,157)&&&
\end{array}
\]
For each row, direct addition gives \(p+q=4k+2\). All the displayed numbers are prime. This can be checked by trial division: for each displayed number it is enough to test prime divisors not exceeding its square root (the largest number occurring is \(233\), so only \(2,3,5,7,11,13\) need be considered). Thus the required Goldbach decomposition holds for every \(1\le k<60\).

### The range \(k\ge60\)

Set
\[
 n=2k+1.
\]
This number is odd. Moreover, since \(k\ge60\),
\[
 n=2k+1\ge121>120.
\]
Therefore the assumed nonvanishing statement (1) gives
\[
 A(2k+1)\ne0.
 \tag{2}
\]

Suppose, for contradiction, that \(4k+2\) were not a sum of two primes. Since
\[
 4k+2=2(2k+1)=2n,
\]
this says exactly that \(2n\) is not a sum of two primes. The lemma would then imply
\[
 A(n)=A(2k+1)=0,
\]
contradicting (2). Hence \(4k+2\) must be a sum of two primes.

The finite table handles every positive \(k<60\), and the determinant argument handles every \(k\ge60\). Therefore, under the conjecture that \(A(n)\ne0\) for every odd \(n>120\), every integer of the form \(4k+2\) with \(k>0\) is the sum of two primes.
